n: Nephi continues with Isaiah 49. The Book of Mormon has a longer opening than the KJV, addressing scattered Israel “broken off” because of wicked leaders — words that fit Lehi’s family well. Then the Servant speaks: the Lord called him before birth.

f.g: Shepherds — here, Israel’s religious and political leaders.
KJV Isaiah 49:1 begins here; the earlier words are unique to the Book of Mormon.

n: The Servant’s words are like a sharp sword, and God has kept him hidden like a polished arrow in a quiver, ready for the right moment.
God calls the Servant “Israel,” through whom He will be glorified. The Servant can be understood as Israel as a people, a prophet, and ultimately Jesus Christ, the perfect Servant.
The Servant feels his labor has been in vain, yet trusts that God will judge and reward his work. Many faithful servants feel this discouragement.
Though Israel is not yet gathered, the Servant will be honored by the Lord, who will be his strength.

f.w: to bring Jacob again to him

n: Restoring Israel is too small a task: the Servant will also be a light to the Gentiles, bringing God’s salvation to the ends of the earth.
The Servant, despised and hated by the nations, will one day be honored by kings and princes who rise and bow. The Book of Mormon reads “to servant of rulers” (KJV “to a servant of rulers”).

In a time of favor God helps His people and gives His Servant as a covenant to restore desolate lands. The Book of Mormon adds “O isles of the sea” and “my servant,” making clear that the scattered remnants, like Lehi’s family, are included.
The Servant will free prisoners and call those in darkness into the light — an image Latter-day Saints also connect with Christ’s work for the dead.

f.w: say to the prisoners: Go forth

n: Those returning will never hunger or thirst. Their merciful Shepherd will lead them to springs of water.

f.w: They shall not hunger nor thirst

n: God will turn the mountains into roads and raise up highways for the gathering.
Israel will be gathered from far away: north, west, and the land of Sinim.

f.g: A distant land; some scholars link it to Syene (Aswan) in southern Egypt, others to China.

n: Heaven and earth are invited to sing because God comforts His people. The Book of Mormon adds that those in the east will be established and “smitten no more.”
Zion feels abandoned and forgotten. The Book of Mormon adds a reassurance: “but he will show that he hath not.”
One of scripture’s most tender images: even if a nursing mother could forget her baby, God will never forget Israel. The Book of Mormon adds “O house of Israel.”

f.w: can a woman forget her sucking child

n: God has engraved Israel on the palms of His hands. Christians see a reminder of Christ’s nail-scarred hands, which He showed to His disciples after the Resurrection.

f.w: graven thee upon the palms of my hands

n: Zion’s children will hurry home, and those who destroyed her will leave.

f.g: Hurry; the Hebrew can also mean “builders,” a play on words.

n: Look around: Zion’s children are gathering. She will wear them like ornaments or a bride’s jewelry.
Zion’s ruined land will become too crowded for all its people, and her enemies will be far away.

f.w: too narrow by reason of the inhabitants

n: The children born after Zion’s losses will say the land is too cramped and ask for more room.
Zion, amazed, asks where all these children came from when she had been bereaved, captive, and alone.
God will raise His banner to the Gentiles, who will carry Israel’s sons and daughters home. Nephi explains in the next chapter that this means Gentile nations helping gather Israel.

f.g: Raise a banner or flag as a rallying point.

n: Kings and queens will become Israel’s caretakers. Bowing low depicts honoring Israel, and those who wait for the Lord will never be ashamed.

f.w: they shall not be ashamed that wait for me

n: A question: can captives be taken from a mighty warrior? Normally, no.

f.g: Captives held by a powerful or rightful captor.

n: But God will free even the captives of the mighty. He will fight those who fight Israel and save her children.

f.w: I will contend with him that contendeth with thee

n: Israel’s oppressors will destroy one another — a vivid poetic picture of self-destructive evil. Then all will know that the Lord is Israel’s Savior and Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

f.w: feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh
